claim: RoxS is a major trans-acting sRNA shared between Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus aureus
source: We show that Bacillus subtilis RoxS, a major trans-acting sRNA shared with Staphylococus aureus, prevents degradation of the yflS mRNA, encoding a malate transporter.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of RoxS

claim: RoxS prevents degradation of the yflS mRNA
source: We show that Bacillus subtilis RoxS, a major trans-acting sRNA shared with Staphylococus aureus, prevents degradation of the yflS mRNA, encoding a malate transporter.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot experiments showing increased yflS mRNA half-life in presence of RoxS

claim: yflS mRNA encodes a malate transporter
source: We show that Bacillus subtilis RoxS, a major trans-acting sRNA shared with Staphylococus aureus, prevents degradation of the yflS mRNA, encoding a malate transporter.
evidence: Referenced from prior literature (Tanaka et al., 2003)

claim: RoxS expression is induced in the presence of malate
source: In the presence of malate, RoxS transiently escapes from repression by the NADH-sensitive transcription factor Rex and binds to the extreme 5'-end of yflS mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated by Northern blot analysis showing increased RoxS levels after malate addition

claim: RoxS is repressed by the NADH-sensitive transcription factor Rex
source: In the presence of malate, RoxS transiently escapes from repression by the NADH-sensitive transcription factor Rex and binds to the extreme 5'-end of yflS mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blots and EMSA showing Rex binding to RoxS promoter

claim: RoxS binds to the extreme 5'-end of yflS mRNA
source: In the presence of malate, RoxS transiently escapes from repression by the NADH-sensitive transcription factor Rex and binds to the extreme 5'-end of yflS mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated through structure probing, compensatory mutations, and in vitro protection assays

claim: RoxS impairs the 5'-3' exoribonuclease activity of RNase J1
source: This impairs the 5'-3' exoribonuclease activity of RNase J1, increasing the half-life of the primary transcript and concomitantly enhancing ribosome binding to increase expression of the transporter.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro RNase J1 degradation assays and in vivo half-life measurements in RNase J1 mutants

claim: RoxS increases the half-life of the yflS primary transcript
source: This impairs the 5'-3' exoribonuclease activity of RNase J1, increasing the half-life of the primary transcript and concomitantly enhancing ribosome binding to increase expression of the transporter.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot half-life measurements showing 3.6-fold stabilization

claim: RoxS enhances ribosome binding to yflS mRNA
source: This impairs the 5'-3' exoribonuclease activity of RNase J1, increasing the half-life of the primary transcript and concomitantly enhancing ribosome binding to increase expression of the transporter.
evidence: Demonstrated through toeprinting assays showing increased 30S ribosomal subunit binding

claim: RoxS increases expression of the YflS transporter
source: This impairs the 5'-3' exoribonuclease activity of RNase J1, increasing the half-life of the primary transcript and concomitantly enhancing ribosome binding to increase expression of the transporter.
evidence: Demonstrated through β-galactosidase assays of yflS-lacZ translational fusion

claim: RoxS helps readjust the cellular NAD+/NADH balance when perturbed by different stimuli
source: Globally, the different targets regulated by RoxS suggest that it helps readjust the cellular NAD+/NADH balance when perturbed by different stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the regulation of multiple targets involved in NAD+/NADH metabolism and Rex-mediated control

claim: E. coli depends primarily on endonucleolytic cleavage by RNase E to initiate RNA turnover
source: E. coli depends primarily on endonucleolytic cleavage by RNase E to initiate RNA turnover, followed by degradation of the resulting fragments in a 3'-to-5' orientation by exoribonucleases.
evidence: Cited from established literature on E. coli RNA degradation

claim: B. subtilis has replaced RNase E by an enzyme with similar properties called RNase Y
source: B. subtilis, on the other hand, has replaced RNase E by an enzyme with similar properties called RNase Y and has the additional option of exonucleolytically degrading RNAs from the 5' end using an enzyme called RNase J1 (Mathy et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Mathy et al., 2007 and established knowledge of B. subtilis RNA degradation

claim: B. subtilis can exonucleolytically degrade RNAs from the 5' end using RNase J1
source: B. subtilis, on the other hand, has replaced RNase E by an enzyme with similar properties called RNase Y and has the additional option of exonucleolytically degrading RNAs from the 5' end using an enzyme called RNase J1 (Mathy et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Mathy et al., 2007

claim: Only eight of the >30 ribonucleases currently identified in E. coli and B. subtilis are present in both organisms
source: Only eight of the >30 ribonucleases currently identified in these two bacteria are present in both organisms.
evidence: Cited from comparative studies of ribonucleases (Bechhofer, 2009; Durand et al., 2015b; Condon and Putzer, 2002)

claim: In E. coli, sRNAs generally act by imperfect base pairing with their target mRNAs
source: In these organisms, sRNAs generally act by an imperfect base pairing with their target mRNAs.
evidence: Established knowledge from sRNA literature

claim: The interaction between sRNA and mRNA often requires the chaperone Hfq in Gram-negative bacteria
source: The interaction between sRNA and mRNA often requires the chaperone Hfq, an Sm-like protein that both stabilizes the sRNA and facilitates the pairing with mRNA targets (for review, see Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from review by Updegrove et al., 2016

claim: Hfq stabilizes sRNAs and facilitates pairing with mRNA targets
source: The interaction between sRNA and mRNA often requires the chaperone Hfq, an Sm-like protein that both stabilizes the sRNA and facilitates the pairing with mRNA targets (for review, see Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from review by Updegrove et al., 2016

claim: Most sRNAs examined to date directly affect mRNA translation with an indirect effect on mRNA half-life
source: In bacteria, most sRNAs examined to date directly affect mRNA translation with an indirect effect on mRNA half-life (reviewed in Wagner and Romby, 2015).
evidence: Cited from review by Wagner and Romby, 2015

claim: Some sRNAs can directly affect mRNA stability without affecting translation
source: However, some more recent studies have shown that sRNAs are also able to directly affect mRNA stability without affecting translation, by recruiting the degradation machinery or interfering with its action (reviewed in Lalaouna et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from review by Lalaouna et al., 2013

claim: The sRNA MicC can recruit RNase E to the ompD mRNA
source: In one particular example, the ternary complex formed between the sRNA (MicC), the mRNA (ompD) and Hfq can recruit RNase E to a site within the open reading frame and stimulate its cleavage by presenting the 5' monophosphate of the sRNA to RNase E (Bandyra et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Bandyra et al., 2012

claim: The sRNA RydC increases the stability of the cfa mRNA by hiding a cleavage site from RNase E
source: In another, the sRNA RydC increases the stability of the cfa mRNA by pairing to the 5'-UTR of this mRNA, far upstream of the ribosome binding site, and hiding a cleavage site from RNase E (Fröhlich et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Fröhlich et al., 2013

claim: In B. subtilis, Hfq is generally not required for sRNA-mRNA pairing
source: In these bacteria, Hfq is generally not required for sRNA-mRNA pairing (Hämmerle et al., 2014; Rochat et al., 2015) although there are some exceptions in specific organisms (Nielsen et al., 2010; Boudry et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Hämmerle et al., 2014 and Rochat et al., 2015

claim: RoxS is the unique trans-acting sRNA, apart from 6S RNA, that is conserved between B. subtilis and S. aureus
source: RoxS (related to oxidative stress) is the unique trans-acting sRNA, apart from the ubiquitous 6S RNA, that is conserved between B. subtilis and the Gram-positive pathogen S. aureus.
evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claim: In S. aureus, RoxS (RsaE) regulates genes involved in amino acid and peptide transport, cofactor synthesis, lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism and the TCA cycle
source: First identified in S. aureus where it is named RsaE, it was shown to regulate genes involved in amino acid and peptide transport, cofactor synthesis, lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism and the TCA cycle (Geissmann et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Geissmann et al., 2009

claim: RoxS transcription is induced during nitric oxide (NO) stress by the two-component system ResDE
source: In a previous study, we showed that RoxS transcription is induced during nitric oxide (NO) stress by the two-component system ResDE and regulates the expression of numerous genes linked to oxido-reduction processes in B. subtilis (Durand et al., 2015a).
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work (Durand et al., 2015a)

claim: RoxS regulates the expression of numerous genes linked to oxido-reduction processes in B. subtilis
source: In a previous study, we showed that RoxS transcription is induced during nitric oxide (NO) stress by the two-component system ResDE and regulates the expression of numerous genes linked to oxido-reduction processes in B. subtilis (Durand et al., 2015a).
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work (Durand et al., 2015a)

claim: This is the first known case of an sRNA controlling 5'-exoribonuclease activity in bacteria
source: This is the first known case of an sRNA controlling 5'-exoribonuclease activity in bacteria.
evidence: Based on literature review and novelty of findings

claim: RoxS expression is controlled by Rex, a transcriptional repressor of genes linked to fermentation processes that senses the NAD+/NADH balance in the cell
source: Lastly, we show that RoxS expression is controlled by Rex, a transcriptional repressor of genes linked to fermentation processes that senses the NAD+/NADH balance in the cell.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blots in Rex mutant and EMSA showing Rex binding to RoxS promoter

claim: The yflS mRNA has a transcriptional start site 5 or 6 nts downstream of the predicted -10 region
source: The primer extension product obtained with the yflS-specific oligonucleotide mapped to two consecutive residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the yflS mRNA can start at an A or G residue, 5 or 6 nts downstream of the predicted −10 region, and thus has a 38/39 nt 5'-UTR.
evidence: Demonstrated through primer extension assays with Xrn1 treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The yflS mRNA has a 38/39 nt 5'-UTR
source: The primer extension product obtained with the yflS-specific oligonucleotide mapped to two consecutive residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the yflS mRNA can start at an A or G residue, 5 or 6 nts downstream of the predicted −10 region, and thus has a 38/39 nt 5'-UTR.
evidence: Calculated from primer extension mapping data

claim: The yflS promoter and 5'-UTR is highly conserved among Bacilli with a clearly identifiable yflS gene
source: This promoter and 5'-UTR is highly conserved among Bacilli with a clearly identifiable yflS gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The yflS gene encodes a malate transporter whose expression is induced by the two-component system MalKR
source: The yflS gene encodes a malate transporter whose expression is induced by the two-component system (MalKR), which senses the presence of malate in the medium (Tanaka et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Tanaka et al., 2003

claim: The half-life of the yflS mRNA is 2.5 min in a WT strain
source: The half-life of the yflS mRNA was 2.5 min in a WT strain but decreased to 0.7 min in the absence of RoxS.
evidence: Measured through Northern blot analysis after rifampicin addition

claim: The half-life of the yflS mRNA decreases to 0.7 min in the absence of RoxS
source: The half-life of the yflS mRNA was 2.5 min in a WT strain but decreased to 0.7 min in the absence of RoxS.
evidence: Measured through Northern blot analysis after rifampicin addition

claim: RoxS stabilizes the yflS mRNA about 3.6-fold
source: Thus, RoxS stabilizes the yflS mRNA about 3.6-fold, presumably by protecting it from degradation by cellular RNases.
evidence: Calculated from half-life measurements (2.5 min / 0.7 min)

claim: Deletion of RNase III has no major impact on yflS mRNA half-life in either the presence or absence of RoxS
source: Deletion of the gene encoding RNase III (∆rnc) had no major impact on yflS mRNA half-life in either the presence (3.1 min) or absence (0.7 min) of RoxS (Figure 2B compared to Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot half-life measurements in RNase III mutant strains

claim: RNase Y plays a major role in yflS mRNA turnover
source: This result shows that RNase Y plays a major role in yflS mRNA turnover.
evidence: Demonstrated by 10-fold stabilization of yflS mRNA in RNase Y mutant

claim: RoxS does not protect the full-length yflS transcript from attack by RNase Y
source: This suggests that RoxS does not protect the full-length yflS transcript from attack by RNase Y and that the effect of RNase Y on yflS turnover is RoxS-independent.
evidence: Inferred from similar stabilization in RNase Y mutant regardless of RoxS presence

claim: Deletion of RoxS no longer destabilizes the full-length yflS mRNA in the ∆rnjA background
source: Remarkably, however, deletion of RoxS no longer destabilized the full-length yflS mRNA in the ∆rnjA background (4 vs 3.8 min half-lives in ∆rnjA and ∆roxS ∆rnjA strains, respectively).
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot half-life measurements in RNase J1 mutant strains

claim: RoxS protects the full-length yflS mRNA from degradation by RNase J1 in vivo
source: Thus, RoxS protects the full-length yflS mRNA from degradation by RNase J1 in vivo.
evidence: Concluded from loss of RoxS effect in RNase J1 mutant background

claim: RNase J1 is inhibited by the tri-phosphate group present on the 5' end of primary transcripts
source: RNase J1 is known to be inhibited by the tri-phosphate group present on the 5' end of primary transcripts (Mathy et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Mathy et al., 2007

claim: RppH is the only known enzyme to catalyze conversion of 5' tri-phosphate to mono-phosphate in B. subtilis
source: To date, the only known enzyme to catalyze this reaction in B. subtilis is the RNA pyrophosphohydrolase RppH (Richards et al., 2011), although other as yet unidentified enzymes are thought to have similar activity.
evidence: Cited from Richards et al., 2011

claim: BsRppH prefers a guanosine residue in the second position of its RNA substrates
source: BsRppH prefers a guanosine residue in the second position of its RNA substrates (Piton et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Piton et al., 2013

claim: RppH is not the enzyme responsible for the removal of the 5' tri-phosphate of yflS mRNA
source: Thus, RppH is not the enzyme responsible for the removal of the 5' tri-phosphate of yflS mRNA to give access to RNase J1.
evidence: Demonstrated through half-life measurements in RppH mutant showing no change in RoxS effect

claim: Other RNA pyrophosphohydrolase activities are waiting to be identified in B. subtilis
source: This result is consistent with the idea that other RNA pyrophosphohydrolase activities are waiting to be identified in B. subtilis.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that RppH is not responsible for yflS 5' processing but processing still occurs

claim: RoxS protects the 5' end of yflS from RNase J1 degradation in vitro
source: In contrast, almost no AMP was visible when the reaction was performed in the presence of RoxS, showing clearly that the 5' end of yflS is protected from RNase J1 by the sRNA (Figure 3, lanes 8–11).
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro RNase J1 degradation assays shown in Figure 3

claim: RoxS has four C-rich regions (CRRs) that can potentially base-pair with G-rich complementary sequences in its targets
source: RoxS has four C-rich regions (CRRs) that can potentially base-pair with G-rich complementary sequences in its targets (Figure 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1 structure diagram

claim: RoxS mainly uses CRR3 to regulate the expression of the ppnkB mRNA
source: In our previous work, we showed that RoxS mainly uses CRR3 to regulate the expression of the ppnkB mRNA (Durand et al., 2015a).
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work (Durand et al., 2015a)

claim: The CRR3 region of RoxS is the key C-rich motif for the initiation of base-pairing and protection of the 5' end of the yflS mRNA
source: These results suggest that the CRR3 region of RoxS is the key C-rich motif for the initiation of base-pairing and protection of the 5' end of the yflS mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated through mutational analysis showing loss of protection with CRR3 mutants

claim: Compensatory mutations in RoxS CRR3 and yflS 5' end restore protection from RNase J1
source: Even though the yflSmut5' RNA was intrinsically a better substrate for RNase J1 than yflSWT, wild-type RoxS similarly showed weaker protection of the yflSmut5' RNA than the CRR3-2 compensatory mutant (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro RNase J1 degradation assays with compensatory mutants shown in Figure 4

claim: RoxS primarily uses the CRR3 region to hybridize to yflS mRNA
source: Together, these observations show convincingly that, as for the ppnKB mRNA, RoxS primarily uses the CRR3 region to hybridize to yflS mRNA.
evidence: Demonstrated through structure probing showing changes in CRR3 region upon yflS binding

claim: RoxS binding induces a long-range perturbation of the yflS mRNA structure close to the SD sequence
source: These results strongly support the prediction that RoxS base-pairs with the extreme 5' end of the yflS mRNA through CRR3, and suggest that RoxS additionally induces a long-range perturbation of the mRNA structure close to the SD sequence.
evidence: Inferred from structure probing showing changes near SD sequence upon RoxS binding

claim: RoxS stimulates the formation of the translation initiation complex on yflS mRNA
source: Addition of wild-type RoxS or the CRR1 mutant increased the signal at +16 approximately 3-fold, suggesting that RoxS stimulates the formation of the translation initiation complex.
evidence: Demonstrated through toeprinting assays showing increased 30S ribosomal subunit binding

claim: RoxS stimulates YflS synthesis in vivo
source: After 60 min induction, the specific ß-galactosidase activity was 2-fold higher in a WT background compared to the RoxS mutant strain, showing that RoxS stimulates YflS synthesis in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated through β-galactosidase assays of yflS-lacZ translational fusion

claim: RoxS-mediated stimulation of yflS mRNA translation and its protection from RNase J1 are independent phenomena
source: These results suggest that the stimulation of translation by RoxS is not a prerequisite for the protection of yflS mRNA from RNase J1. In other words, RoxS-mediated stimulation of yflS mRNA translation and its protection from RNase J1 are independent phenomena.
evidence: Demonstrated through half-life measurements of non-translated yflS variant showing RoxS still stabilizes the mRNA

claim: RoxS levels increase for about 30 min after addition of glucose before falling again at the 60 min time point
source: RoxS levels increased for about 30 min after addition of glucose before falling again at the 60 min time point.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot time course after glucose addition

claim: Addition of malate to the medium causes a much greater increase in RoxS levels than glucose
source: A similar profile, but of much greater amplitude was seen upon addition of malate to the medium and addition of both carbon sources together (malate + glucose) had a cumulative effect on RoxS levels.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot time course after malate addition

claim: Addition of both malate and glucose together has a cumulative effect on RoxS levels
source: A similar profile, but of much greater amplitude was seen upon addition of malate to the medium and addition of both carbon sources together (malate + glucose) had a cumulative effect on RoxS levels.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot time course after addition of both carbon sources

claim: ResDE is not involved in the induction of RoxS expression by malate
source: However, RoxS levels were still inducible by malate in the absence of ResDE, with the same kinetics as in the WT strain, showing that ResDE is not involved in this regulation.
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot in ResDE mutant showing malate still induces RoxS

claim: The effect of the MalKR two-component system on RoxS levels is indirect
source: These data suggest that the effect of the MalKR two-component system on RoxS levels is indirect.
evidence: Inferred from lack of MalR binding to RoxS promoter despite loss of malate induction in MalKR mutant

claim: Rex represses RoxS transcription
source: This result suggests that Rex represses RoxS transcription and that addition of malate to the growth medium causes a transient release from this repression for at least 30 mins (see discussion).
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blots showing high RoxS levels in Rex mutant and EMSA showing Rex binding to RoxS promoter

claim: Addition of malate to the growth medium causes a transient release from Rex-mediated repression of RoxS
source: This result suggests that Rex represses RoxS transcription and that addition of malate to the growth medium causes a transient release from this repression for at least 30 mins (see discussion).
evidence: Inferred from Northern blot time course showing transient increase in RoxS after malate addition

claim: Rex can directly bind the RoxS promoter region
source: We also obtained a gel-shifted species for the roxS promoter fragment, confirming that Rex can directly bind this promoter region and explaining how it can inhibit transcription.
evidence: Demonstrated through EMSA showing Rex binding to RoxS promoter DNA

claim: The Rex protein and its predicted binding site just downstream of the roxS promoter are conserved in S. aureus and Staphylococcaceae
source: Interestingly, the Rex protein and its predicted binding site just downstream of the roxS promoter are conserved in S. aureus and in Staphylococcaceae in general (Pagels et al., 2010), suggesting similar regulation may occur in these pathogenic bacteria (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through sequence alignment shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and cited from Pagels et al., 2010

claim: RoxS destabilizes the ppnkB mRNA about 20-fold in the presence of malate
source: In 2xTY plus malate, however, RoxS destabilized the ppnkB mRNA about 20-fold and the sucD mRNA about 8-fold (Figure 11B).
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot half-life measurements in presence of malate

claim: RoxS destabilizes the sucD mRNA about 8-fold in the presence of malate
source: In 2xTY plus malate, however, RoxS destabilized the ppnkB mRNA about 20-fold and the sucD mRNA about 8-fold (Figure 11B).
evidence: Demonstrated through Northern blot half-life measurements in presence of malate

claim: RoxS has a far greater impact on gene expression in the presence of malate
source: This result confirms our previous data and shows that RoxS has a far greater impact on gene expression in the presence of malate.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing effects on ppnkB and sucD mRNA stability with and without malate

claim: The RNA binding channel that leads to the RNase J1 catalytic site is only long enough to accommodate 4–5 nts of single stranded RNA
source: The inhibitory effect on RNase J1 5'−3' exoribonuclease activity can easily be understood in structural terms; the RNA binding channel that leads to the RNase J1 catalytic site is only long enough to accommodate 4–5 nts of single stranded RNA.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of RNase J1

claim: The unbound yflS mRNA is predicted to have at least six unpaired nts before the first hairpin structure
source: The unbound yflS mRNA is predicted to have at least six unpaired nts before the first hairpin structure (Figure 5) and would thus be expected to be a good substrate for RNase J1 once the 5'-triphosphate group has been removed.
evidence: Predicted from structure probing data shown in Figure 5

claim: When bound to RoxS, the duplexed 5' end of the yflS RNA can no longer reach the RNase J1 catalytic site
source: When bound to RoxS, the duplexed 5' end of the yflS RNA can no longer reach the catalytic site, explaining how it is protected from degradation.
evidence: Inferred from structural constraints of RNase J1 and base-pairing between RoxS and yflS

claim: In Clostridium perfringens, the colA mRNA is stabilized by the VR-RNA
source: Obana et al. (2010, 2013) showed that the Clostridium perfringens colA mRNA (encoding collagenase) is stabilized by the VR-RNA.
evidence: Cited from Obana et al., 2010, 2013

claim: In Streptococcus pyogenes, the FasX sRNA stabilizes the streptokinase encoding mRNA (ska)
source: In the pathogen Streptococcus pyogenes, the FasX sRNA stabilizes the streptokinase encoding mRNA (ska) (Ramirez-Peña et al., 2010) by binding to its extreme 5' end via a sequence resembling that of the RoxS CRR3 (four consecutive C's matched with four consecutive G's).
evidence: Cited from Ramirez-Peña et al., 2010

claim: RNase J1 is a prime candidate for FasX regulation of the ska mRNA
source: Our data would suggest that RNase J1 is a prime candidate for FasX regulation of the ska mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of FasX-ska interaction to RoxS-yflS interaction

claim: The sRNA-dependent 5' end protection mechanism could be used to activate expression of any mRNA in any microorganism by shielding it from enzymes requiring a single stranded 5' extremity
source: In fact, the sRNA-dependent 5' end protection mechanism discovered here could in theory be used to activate expression of any mRNA in any microorganism by shielding it from enzymes (e.g. RppH, RNase J1, RNase E) requiring a single stranded 5' extremity to initiate degradation.
evidence: Speculated based on the general mechanism discovered

claim: Stabilization of the yflS mRNA and increased translation go hand in hand to produce more of the YflS transporter in the presence of malate
source: However, in all likelihood, the two events are indissociable in vivo with the wild-type yflS mRNA, that is, stabilization of the mRNA and increased translation go hand in hand to produce more of the YflS transporter in the presence of malate.
evidence: Inferred from combined effects of RoxS on both stability and translation

claim: The 3D structure of yflS leader and the impact of RoxS may be more complex than simple secondary structure models
source: This suggests that the 3D structure of yflS leader and the impact of RoxS may be more complex than the model presented in Figure 5.
evidence: Inferred from structure probing data that doesn't fully match predicted secondary structure

claim: The yflS mRNA sequence contains several stretches of consecutive G-residues in the first 50 nts that could potentially form G-quadruplex RNA structures
source: The yflS mRNA sequence contains several stretches of consecutive G-residues in the first 50 nts that could potentially form G-quadruplex RNA structures (Kikin et al., 2006).
evidence: Speculated based on sequence analysis and cited from Kikin et al., 2006

claim: Part of the 5' leader of yflS mRNA could potentially form a triple helix with the stem of the adjacent hairpin
source: Alternatively, part of the 5' leader including the AAACAA sequence (nts 12–17) of yflS mRNA could potentially form a triple helix with the stem of the adjacent hairpin rich in AU pairings.
evidence: Speculated based on sequence analysis

claim: RoxS binding disrupts a particular fold of the 5'UTR that is unfavorable to ribosome recruitment
source: Our structure probing data are consistent with a model in which the duplex formed by binding of RoxS to the 5' end of the yflS mRNA not only blocks RNase J1 access but also disrupts a particular fold of the 5'UTR that is unfavorable to ribosome recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from structure probing and toeprinting data

claim: The temporary release from Rex-mediated repression of RoxS expression may be linked to the generation of NADH in the early steps of malate metabolism
source: The temporary release from Rex-mediated repression of RoxS expression may be linked to the generation of NADH in the early steps of malate metabolism, either in the conversion of malate to oxaloacetate by malate dehydrogenase (Mdh) in the TCA cycle, or its conversion to pyruvate by the malic enzymes MaeA, MalS and MleA (Doan et al., 2003; Lerondel et al., 2006; Meyer and Stülke, 2013) (Figure 12).
evidence: Inferred from Rex's role as NADH sensor and malate metabolism pathways, cited from Doan et al., 2003; Lerondel et al., 2006; Meyer and Stülke, 2013

claim: B. subtilis has at least four malate transporters: MaeN, YflS, MleN, and CimH
source: B. subtilis has at least four malate transporters: MaeN (Wei et al., 2000) and YflS (Tanaka et al., 2003), both regulated by the two-component system MalKR (Tanaka et al., 2003), and MleN (Wei et al., 2000) and CimH, the latter of which is primarily a transporter of citrate (Sobczak and Lolkema, 2005).
evidence: Cited from Wei et al., 2000; Tanaka et al., 2003; Sobczak and Lolkema, 2005

claim: Malate is a common source of carbon for B. subtilis in its natural habitat since it is released by the roots of many plants
source: Malate is a common source of carbon for B. subtilis in its natural habitat since it is released by the roots of many plants (Rudrappa et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Rudrappa et al., 2008

claim: Most of the malate imported by B. subtilis cells serves in gluconeogenesis and the excess is sent towards overflow metabolism/fermentation
source: Most of the malate imported by B. subtilis cells serves in gluconeogenesis and the excess is sent towards overflow metabolism/fermentation and the production of lactate, acetate, acetoin and 2,3-butanediol (Kleijn et al., 2010) (Figure 12).
evidence: Cited from Kleijn et al., 2010

claim: Overflow metabolism/fermentation allows NAD+ regeneration, primarily catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh/LctE)
source: This overflow metabolism/fermentation allows NAD+ regeneration, primarily catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh/LctE) that converts pyruvate to lactate (Cruz Ramos et al., 2000) (Figure 12).
evidence: Cited from Cruz Ramos et al., 2000

claim: Transcription of the maeN mRNA is essentially turned off during fermentation and ethanol stress
source: Transcription of the maeN mRNA, encoding the main malate transporter, is essentially turned off during fermentation and ethanol stress (Nicolas et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Nicolas et al., 2012

claim: RoxS specifically stabilizes the yflS mRNA to compensate for the decrease in maeN expression during fermentation
source: It is possible that RoxS specifically stabilizes the yflS mRNA to compensate for this decrease in maeN expression, thus facilitating the continued uptake of malate during conditions where the fermentation/overflow pathway is turned on.
evidence: Speculated based on the complementary regulation of malate transporters

claim: 30% of genes with increased expression in a ∆roxS strain are linked to oxido-reduction processes
source: Our previous study showed that 30% of genes with increased expression in a ∆roxS strain are linked to oxido-reduction processes (Durand et al., 2015a).
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work (Durand et al., 2015a)

claim: RoxS down-regulates ppnKB, encoding NAD-kinase
source: Its down-regulated targets include ppnKB, encoding NAD-kinase, and the TCA cycle components sucCD and citZ.
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work

claim: RoxS down-regulates the TCA cycle components sucCD and citZ
source: Its down-regulated targets include ppnKB, encoding NAD-kinase, and the TCA cycle components sucCD and citZ.
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work

claim: PpnKB and the TCA cycle are significant contributors to the production of NADPH and NADH, respectively
source: PpnKB and the TCA cycle are significant contributors to the production of NADPH and NADH, respectively (Figure 12).
evidence: Based on established metabolic knowledge

claim: A key role of RoxS is to temporarily turn down part of the TCA cycle to help restore the NAD+/NADH balance
source: These observations, together with the fact that RoxS is regulated by the NADH-sensitive transcriptional repressor Rex, suggest that a key role of RoxS is to temporarily turn down part of the TCA cycle to help restore the NAD+/NADH balance.
evidence: Inferred from RoxS regulation of TCA cycle components and Rex-mediated control

claim: Once the NAD+/NADH ratio is restored, Rex would be predicted to become active again as a repressor
source: Once the NAD+/NADH ratio is restored, Rex would be predicted to become active again as a repressor, explaining the decrease in RoxS levels seen in Northern blots about one hour after addition of malate and the loss of this down-regulation in the Rex mutant (Figure 9D).
evidence: Inferred from Rex mechanism and observed RoxS expression kinetics

claim: Expression of the lactate dehydrogenase gene (ldh) is up-regulated in ∆roxS cells
source: In further agreement with a role for RoxS in managing NADH levels, we showed in our previous report that expression of the lactate dehydrogenase gene (ldh) and the cydA gene, encoding a subunit of cytochrome bd, is up-regulated in ∆roxS cells (Durand et al., 2015a).
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work (Durand et al., 2015a)

claim: Expression of the cydA gene, encoding a subunit of cytochrome bd, is up-regulated in ∆roxS cells
source: In further agreement with a role for RoxS in managing NADH levels, we showed in our previous report that expression of the lactate dehydrogenase gene (ldh) and the cydA gene, encoding a subunit of cytochrome bd, is up-regulated in ∆roxS cells (Durand et al., 2015a).
evidence: Cited from authors' previous work (Durand et al., 2015a)

claim: Neither ldh nor cydA mRNAs are predicted to be direct targets of RoxS
source: Neither of these mRNAs is predicted to be a direct target of RoxS, but both are members of the Rex regulon.
evidence: Based on target prediction analysis and knowledge of Rex regulon

claim: The increased expression of ldh and cydA is indicative of higher intracellular NADH levels and Rex derepression in the ∆roxS strain
source: Their increased expression is thus most likely indicative of higher intracellular NADH levels and Rex derepression in the ∆roxS strain.
evidence: Inferred from Rex mechanism and indirect regulation

claim: A link between NO levels and regulation of virulence via NADH and Rex has been proposed in S. aureus
source: Interestingly, a link between NO levels and regulation of virulence via NADH and Rex has been proposed in S. aureus (Pagels et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Pagels et al., 2010

claim: The conservation of the Rex binding site downstream of the RsaE/RoxS promoter in S. aureus suggests that this pathway is evolutionarily conserved
source: The conservation of the Rex binding site downstream of the RsaE/RoxS promoter in S. aureus suggests that this pathway is evolutionarily conserved to best serve the adaptation of B. subtilis and S. aureus to their respective niches.
evidence: Inferred from sequence conservation analysis
